::: {.callout-note title="Running the code in this tutorial"}
Every code chunk here is tagged with `#| eval: false`, so the published page shows the code **without running it**. To run it yourself, open the downloaded `.qmd` in **RStudio**:

- **Run one chunk:** click the green ▶ (*Run Current Chunk*) at the chunk's top-right, or press *Ctrl/Cmd + Enter*. This runs the chunk **regardless of its `eval` setting** — the easiest way to work through the tutorial interactively.
- **Run a chunk on render:** change that chunk's `#| eval: false` to `#| eval: true` (or delete the line) so it executes when the document is rendered.
- **Render the whole tutorial:** click the **Render** button in RStudio (or run `quarto render` in a terminal) to execute the chunks top-to-bottom and knit a finished HTML. To run everything on render, set `eval: true` once in the YAML header at the top.
:::


## About this tutorial

This is the **runnable companion** to the P1 reading — the first hour of the optional **Tuesday (Day 0)** computational refresher. The reading builds the mental model (how computers work, what an HPC cluster is, what Talapas is); here you actually **do it**: install and open VS Code, connect it to the University of Oregon's **Talapas** cluster over Remote-SSH, start an **interactive** compute session, find your way around the Talapas file systems, and run your first R job on a compute node. By the end you will have run a small script on Talapas and opened the PDF and CSV it wrote — proof your connection works before Day 1.

We stop at **interactive mode** today (a shell on a compute node). Writing and submitting **SLURM batch jobs** is the Friday-morning track ([Modules 09–10](../Materials.html)) — not part of this Tuesday session.

::: callout-note
**Companion lecture:** [Lecture P1 — Computer Systems](../Lecture_Folder/Lecture_P1_Computer_Systems.html) · **Companion reading:** [Chapter P1 — Computer Systems](../Resources_Folder/Chapter_P1_Computer_Systems.html).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="How to use this page"}
The rendered HTML shows the commands but does **not** execute them. To work along, download the source — <a href="Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd.txt" download="Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd">Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd</a> — then **drop the trailing `.txt`** so the filename ends in `.qmd`, and open it in **VS Code** (or RStudio). The shell commands are meant to be typed into a terminal connected to Talapas.
:::

## 1. Before you start

You need three things in place before the steps below will work:

1.  A **UO Duck ID** (the part of your UO email before `@uoregon.edu`) and your University-wide UO password.
2.  A **Talapas account** tied to a **PIRG** (Principal Investigator Research Group). Ask your PI to add you to their PIRG, or request access at [racs.uoregon.edu/request-access](https://racs.uoregon.edu/request-access).
3.  If you are **off campus**, connect to the **UO VPN** first — the Talapas login nodes are only reachable from the campus network or the VPN.

Throughout this tutorial, replace `<yourduckid>` with your Duck ID and `<myPIRG>` with your PIRG name. If you are not sure which PIRG you belong to, you will find out in Section 6 by running `groups` once you are logged in.

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
Why do you need a PIRG just to run a job? What is it used for?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

A PIRG is your research group's **account** on Talapas. SLURM (the scheduler) uses it to track and charge resource usage to the right group, and to enforce each group's share of the cluster. Every job you submit — interactive or batch — must name an account with `--account=<myPIRG>`, or it will be rejected. It is the cluster-scale version of the operating-system idea that every process runs under a user/group with specific permissions.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Install and open VS Code

**Visual Studio Code** is a free, cross-platform editor from Microsoft. It lets you browse and edit files — including files on a remote server like Talapas — and its built-in terminal lets you run commands without leaving the editor. That makes it ideal for the workshop.

1.  Download it from <https://code.visualstudio.com/download> and run the installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
2.  Launch VS Code. Allow any permissions it requests on first start.
3.  Take a moment to find the **Activity Bar** down the left edge — the icons there switch between the Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, and (after the next step) Remote Explorer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Install the Remote-SSH and Quarto extensions

In the left **Activity Bar**, click the **Extensions** icon (the four-squares icon), then search for and install:

-   **Remote — SSH** — lets you open folders and run terminals on Talapas.
-   **Remote Explorer** — the sidebar panel for managing SSH hosts.
-   **Quarto** — edit, preview, and run `.qmd` files (the workshop tutorials).

Also handy, so you can open the plots and tables your jobs produce without leaving the editor:

-   an **R** extension (syntax + sending code to an R terminal),
-   a **PDF viewer** and a **CSV/Excel viewer**.

After installing the remote extensions, you should see a new **Remote Explorer** icon in the Activity Bar.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Add the Talapas SSH host

1.  Open **Remote Explorer** from the Activity Bar.
2.  Make sure the dropdown at the top is set to **SSH** (sometimes labelled *SSH Targets*).
3.  Click the **+** ("Add New") icon, and in the prompt that appears type the SSH command below, replacing `<yourduckid>` with your Duck ID:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
ssh <yourduckid>@login.talapas.uoregon.edu
```

4.  Press **Enter**, then **Enter** again to save it to the default SSH config file (`~/.ssh/config`).

`login.talapas.uoregon.edu` now appears as a host under **SSH** in the Remote Explorer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Connect (Duck ID + Duo)

1.  In **Remote Explorer**, find `login.talapas.uoregon.edu` and click the **→** (Connect) arrow — choose to connect in the current window or a new one.
2.  If asked about the platform of the remote host, choose **Linux**.
3.  Enter your **Duck ID password** when prompted. For security, **no characters appear as you type** — that is expected.
4.  When prompted for **Duo**, type `1` and press **Enter** to receive a Duo push (typing `2` sends a text, `3` calls you). Approve the push on your phone.
5.  Once connected, a **green banner** reading **SSH: login.talapas.uoregon.edu** appears in the bottom-left corner of the window.

If the connection hangs or is refused: confirm you are on the **UO VPN** (if off campus), that your Duck ID password is current, and that your Talapas account is active.

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
You are now connected, and the green banner says `login.talapas.uoregon.edu`. Which kind of node are you on — and what are you allowed to do here?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

You are on a **login (head) node**. Login nodes are **shared by everyone** and are for *light* tasks only: browsing and editing files, managing data, and submitting jobs. They are **not** for running real analysis — heavy processes on a login node will be throttled or killed, and they slow the node down for every other user. To do actual computing you must move onto a **compute node**, which you do through SLURM in Section 7.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Open a terminal and explore modules

Open the integrated terminal with **Terminal → New Terminal** (or `` Ctrl+` ``). The prompt will show one of the login nodes (e.g. `login1`).

First, confirm who you are and which PIRG(s) you can charge to:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
whoami                 # your Duck ID
groups                 # your PIRG(s) appear alongside system groups
pwd                    # where am I? -> /home/<yourduckid>
```

Talapas manages centrally installed software with **Lmod** modules. Software is **not** available until you `module load` it — and modules are loaded **per shell**, so you reload them in every new session and in every job script.

```{bash}
#| eval: false
module avail           # list modules you can load right now
module spider R        # search for R and see which versions exist
module load R          # load the default R
module list            # show what is currently loaded
R --version            # confirm R is now on your PATH
module purge           # unload everything (reset) when you want a clean slate
```

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
You ran `R --version` before `module load R` and got "command not found", but after loading it worked. Why isn't R just always available?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

On a shared cluster, many versions of many tools coexist, and different projects need different (sometimes conflicting) versions. Rather than putting everything on everyone's `PATH` at once — which would cause clashes — Talapas keeps software **modular**: nothing analysis-related is loaded by default, and you opt in to exactly what you need with `module load`. Because this happens **per shell**, a fresh terminal (or a new job) starts clean, so you must load your modules again. For reproducibility, pin the version — `module load R/4.4.1` rather than bare `R` — so you get the same R every time.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Start an interactive session

The golden rule: **do not run heavy computation on a login node.** Instead ask SLURM for a compute node. For short, hands-on work the `interactive` partition is ideal. Run (replacing `<myPIRG>`):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
srun --account=<myPIRG> --partition=interactive \
     --time=1:00:00 --mem=4G --pty bash
```

What each piece means:

-   `--account=<myPIRG>` — charge this session to your PIRG (**required**).
-   `--partition=interactive` — the queue for short interactive sessions.
-   `--time=1:00:00` — keep the session for up to 1 hour, then it ends automatically.
-   `--mem=4G` — request 4 GB of RAM (plenty for the tiny demo below).
-   `--pty bash` — give me an interactive `bash` shell.

After a short wait, your prompt changes from `login1` to a compute node name like `n0123`. **That prompt change is how you know you are now on a compute node.** Load R again here, because this is a fresh shell:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
module load R
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Navigate the Talapas file systems

Talapas gives you several places to put files, each with a different purpose and quota. Have a look:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
# Your personal home directory (250 GB) — scripts, small files, dotfiles
cd /home/<yourduckid>
pwd
ls -la

# Your group's shared project space (large, ~2 TB default) — shared data & analysis
ls /projects/<myPIRG>

# High-throughput scratch (20 TB) — fast working space.
# WARNING: files untouched for 90 days are PURGED. Not for anything you can't regenerate.
ls /scratch/<myPIRG>

# Check how much space you're using
df -h ~
du -sh /home/<yourduckid>
```

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
You have a 40 GB intermediate file you'll re-read many times this week, the small R scripts that generate it, and the final figures you want to keep. Where does each belong — `/home`, `/projects`, or `/scratch`?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

- **Scripts and final figures → `/home`** (or `/projects` if the group should share them). `/home` is small (250 GB) but persistent and snapshotted; it is the right place for code and small keepers.
- **The 40 GB intermediate → `/scratch`**. Scratch is large and fast and exactly meant for big working files — but remember the **90-day purge**, so never leave anything there you can't recreate.
- **Anything the whole group needs → `/projects`** (large, shared, more durable than scratch).

And in all cases: **RACS does not back up Talapas** — keep your own backups of anything irreplaceable.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 9. Run your first job: `hello_world.R`

The workshop ships a tiny base-R script that prints where it is running and writes two output files — a PDF plot and a CSV summary. It is at `scripts/hello_world.R` in the Exercise folder. From the Exercise folder (open it with **File → Open Folder…** on Talapas, or `cd` to it in the terminal), run:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
# from inside Exercise_Folder, on your interactive compute node:
Rscript scripts/hello_world.R
```

If you are working from another directory, point at it relative to where you are — for example from `scripts/`'s sibling folder:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
Rscript ../Exercise_Folder/scripts/hello_world.R
```

You should see output like:

``` text
Hello from n0123 at 2026-06-07 10:14:02
R version: R version 4.4.1 ...
Wrote hello_world_plot.pdf and hello_world_summary.csv
```

The script wrote two files in your current directory:

-   `hello_world_plot.pdf` — a simple random-walk plot
-   `hello_world_summary.csv` — a one-row summary table

**Open them in VS Code.** In the Explorer on the left, double-click `hello_world_plot.pdf` (the PDF viewer extension renders it in a tab) and `hello_world_summary.csv` (the CSV viewer shows it as a table). This is the everyday Talapas loop: a job writes outputs, and you inspect them in place without downloading anything.

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
The first line of the output says `Hello from n0123` — not `login1`. Why does that confirm the job ran where it should?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

The script prints the node it is running on (`Sys.info()[["nodename"]]`). Seeing a **compute node** name like `n0123` confirms the work ran on the node SLURM allocated to you in Section 7, **not** on the shared login node. If it had said `login1`, you would have been running computation on the login node — the thing the golden rule tells you never to do.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 10. End the session

When you are done, leave the compute node and return to the login node, then disconnect:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
exit          # ends the interactive srun session; prompt returns to login1
```

Ending the session **releases the compute node** back to the cluster so others can use it (and so your PIRG is not charged for idle time). You can then close the VS Code remote window, or use the green bottom-left banner → **Close Remote Connection** to drop the SSH session entirely.

You now have a working VS Code → Talapas → interactive session → first job loop. For R itself and the command line, continue to the second Tuesday hour: [Tutorial P2 — R & the Command Line](Tutorial_P2_R_and_CommandLine.html).
